planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or early fall in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Cheddar keeps its pale color best where afternoon sun is filtered.

directions: Cheddar is a compact globeflower selection bearing pale, creamy butter-yellow globes rather than the deeper gold of the species, opening above neat mounds of glossy, deeply cut foliage in late spring. Its shorter stature makes it useful toward the front of a moist border or pondside planting where taller globeflowers would flop. Keep the soil constantly moist and site in cool partial shade, since flower color bleaches and plants struggle where summers run hot and dry. Divide every three to four years in early fall to maintain vigor and true color, as seedlings do not come true to the parent.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or early fall in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; a cool, waterside or bog-edge site keeps Lemon Queen flowering well into early summer.

directions: Lemon Queen bears rounded, softly incurved flowers in a clear, cool lemon-yellow, a lighter tone than the golden species that pairs especially well with blues and whites in a moist spring border. The deeply cut, dark green foliage forms a tidy clump that holds its texture through the season if the site never dries out. It shares the species' dislike of heat and drought and performs best in cool climates or at the edge of a pond or stream. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early fall or very early spring to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or early fall in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Alabaster is a vigorous older cultivar that tolerates slightly more sun than most globeflowers if moisture is dependable.

directions: Alabaster produces unusually pale, creamy ivory-white globes that fade almost white in cool weather, a striking departure from the golden tones typical of the genus and an effective foil for bright companions in a moist border. It is a somewhat more vigorous, taller-growing cultivar than newer compact selections, with the same deeply cut, dark green foliage and rounded flower form. Provide the same cool, evenly moist, humus-rich conditions favored by other globeflowers, since performance declines quickly in heat or drought. Divide every three to four years to keep clumps vigorous and floriferous.

planting.note: Plant divisions in early fall or container plants in early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Magnificum goes summer-dormant like the species, so mark its location.

directions: Magnificum is a robust, long-cultivated selection of leopard's bane bearing noticeably larger, brighter golden-yellow daisy flowers than the species type, held on taller stems above heart-shaped, softly hairy basal foliage. Like other leopard's banes it flowers very early, often in March or April, then goes fully dormant by midsummer, so it is best paired with later-emerging perennials such as hostas or ferns that can fill the resulting gap. Provide moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, since the plant declines in hot, dry summer sites. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in late summer, just before fall regrowth begins, to maintain vigor and bloom quality.

common_name: Little Leo Leopard's Bane (Dwarf Compact Doronicum)

planting.note: Plant divisions in early fall or container plants in early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Little Leo's compact habit suits small gardens and container culture better than taller leopard's banes.

directions: Little Leo is a dwarf leopard's bane selection that keeps all the bright, early-spring charm of the species in a much more compact package, forming a low mound of hairy, heart-shaped leaves topped by bright golden-yellow daisies on short stems. Its diminutive size makes it a good choice for the front of a shaded border, rock garden pockets, or edging where the larger species would be out of scale. Like other leopard's banes it flowers very early and then goes dormant by summer, so mark its position and interplant with later-filling shade perennials. Grow in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade and divide congested clumps every two to three years in late summer.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall directly in place; Pulsatilla has a thick taproot and resents transplanting, so avoid disturbing or dividing established plants.

directions: Rubra is a rich wine-red to deep burgundy selection of pasque flower, opening the same silky, upward-then-nodding cups as the species but in a saturated color that stands out sharply against the finely divided, hairy gray-green foliage. It flowers in early spring and is followed by the same feathery, plume-like seedheads that extend the plant's interest well past bloom time. Perfectly drained, lean, gritty, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun is essential, since heavy or waterlogged soil is quickly fatal. Sow fresh seed in fall for best germination and avoid transplanting once established, as the deep taproot resents disturbance.

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall directly in place; Papageno is a mixed-color seed strain, so expect variation in flower shade among seedlings.

directions: Papageno is a distinctive seed strain of pasque flower named for its shaggy, deeply fringed and twisted petals, a striking departure from the smooth-edged cups of the species, blooming in a mix of white, pink, red, and violet-purple shades. The unusual feathery flower form gives plantings a soft, textural quality in early spring, followed by the same ornamental, plume-like seedheads typical of the genus. As with all pasque flowers, perfectly drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun is essential, and the thick taproot resents transplanting once established. Sow fresh seed in fall for the best germination and site where the flowers can be viewed up close.

common_name: Rote Glocke Pasque Flower (Red Bells Pulsatilla)

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall directly in place; this German-bred strain is grown true from carefully selected seed rather than by division.

directions: Rote Glocke ('Red Bells') is a compact German seed strain of pasque flower selected for its deep, glowing wine-red, bell-shaped flowers held just above a low mound of finely dissected, silky-haired foliage. It is more diminutive than many pasque flower selections, making it well suited to trough gardens, rock gardens, and the front edge of a sunny gravel bed. Bloom comes in earliest spring, followed by the genus's characteristic feathery, ornamental seedheads. Grow in perfectly drained, lean, gritty, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun, and sow fresh seed in fall since the deep taproot does not tolerate transplanting or division well.
